item.title: Iran oil cargoes dry up even before US acts on Tehran threats; China's 'teapots' face crunch
item.description: Iranian oil shipments to Asia have nearly dried up as US pressure on Tehran disrupts supplies. Chinese refiners are facing tighter availability, with Iranian crude prices shifting from a discount to a premium of around $4 a barrel.
item.dc:creator: Prabhakar Jha
item.content:encoded: Iran's oil shipments to Asian buyers have nearly dried up, pushing the price of Iranian crude to its highest levels in years as US prepares to announce fresh measures aimed at isolating Tehran and those trading with it.China's private refiners, which have traditionally been the biggest buyers of Iranian oil, are now facing tighter supplies. Iranian crude that was previously sold at a discount to global benchmarks is being offered at a premium of about $4 a barrel, Bloomberg reported.The traders, cited by the Bloomberg, who asked not to be identified because the discussions are private, said the supply squeeze has intensified in recent weeks.Iranian oil supply hits bottleneckA major factor behind the shortage is the impact of US efforts to block Iranian oil shipments. Loaded Iranian tankers have been unable to leave the Persian Gulf, while empty vessels remain stranded outside the region.Data from intelligence firm Kpler showed that about 40 million barrels of Iranian crude were in waters east of peninsular Malaysia, a major storage and transhipment hub for Chinese and other Asian buyers.Only around 4 million barrels of that supply was estimated to remain available for sale, equivalent to roughly two supertankers.The shortage comes ahead of a planned announcement by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on what he has described as "the greatest coordinated economic isolation in the history of the world".Chinese refiners and the financial institutions that facilitate their purchases of Iranian oil could become key targets under the new measures. China faces pressure over Iranian crudeSo far, US sanctions have largely targeted smaller players involved in Iran's oil trade, including private refineries, ports and intermediaries.Washington has also been cautious about aggressively enforcing sanctions against Chinese buyers, partly because of concerns about worsening relations with Beijing and triggering an increase in global oil prices.That approach shifted earlier this year when the US sanctioned Hengli Petrochemical (Dalian) Refinery Co. Ltd., one of China's largest private refiners.China responded by ordering domestic companies not to comply with the sanctions. The US has, however, so far avoided targeting major Chinese banks.At current prices, Iranian crude is trading close to its highest level since the end of the previous Trump administration, according to Emma Li, lead China market analyst at Vortexa."This may prompt teapots to switch back to conventional grades like they did in July or simply reduce runs," Li told Bloomberg.Higher oil prices add to pressure on Chinese refinersThe squeeze on Iranian crude comes as Chinese independent refiners, commonly known as "teapots", are already dealing with weaker demand.Higher benchmark oil prices and longer-term changes such as the growing adoption of electric vehicles have weighed on fuel demand in China.That could make it increasingly difficult for smaller refiners to absorb the higher cost of Iranian crude, potentially pushing them towards alternative grades or lower refinery utilisation.Iran, meanwhile, has continued to withstand decades of US sanctions. Whether a further escalation of economic pressure can force Tehran to change course remains uncertain.Bessent has pledged to target what he calls Iran's "every economic lifeline", arguing that countries and businesses supporting its oil trade could face consequences."Iran's enablers purchase and transport its petroleum. They facilitate the flow of its finances through exchange houses and free trade zones," Bessent wrote in a Financial Times column.He argued that countries supporting Iran's economic network had chosen what they considered the safer option, but warned them to reconsider the consequences.

item.title: China’s J-16 ‘Hidden Dragon’ to face Rafales at ‘Eagles of Civilization’ joint air exercise in Egypt
item.description: China's J-16 fighter jets, also called Hidden Dragon, and the Dassault Rafale are taking part in this year’s Eagles of Civilization joint air exercise in Egypt, according to photos released by the Egyptian Armed Forces (EAF).
item.dc:creator: Akriti Anand
item.content:encoded: China’s advanced J-16 fighter will train alongside France's Rafales in a rare opportunity to test its capabilities against a Western platform, Bloomberg reported on Monday.The J-16 and the Dassault Rafale are taking part in this year’s Eagles of Civilization joint air exercise in Egypt, according to photos released by the Egyptian Armed Forces (EAF).Egypt and China launched the joint 'Eagles of Civilization 2026' air exercise at several air bases across Egypt on Saturday, August 22, 2026, with multirole fighter aircraft of various types taking part, Egypt's State Information Service stated.Notably, the exercise marks the first time China's J-16 heavy fighter jets have travelled to Africa for the China-Egypt joint training. The second edition of the drills began Saturday and will last several days, the EAF said in a statement.Eagles of Civilization 2026 is being held as part of the Egyptian Armed Forces’ joint training program with the militaries of partner countries and is intended to strengthen military cooperation between Egypt and China.About China's J-16 fighter jets: ‘Aerial refueling took place en route to Egypt’The J-16, a twin-seat multi-role fighter nicknamed the ‘Hidden Dragon’, regularly patrols along China’s east coast and potential flashpoints such as the South China Sea and Taiwan Strait, according to South China Morning Post.The jet has previously featured in other overseas drills, including with Russia and Pakistan, but this is the first time it is taking part in an exercise with the Egyptian air force.The J-16 and J-10 are 4.5-generation fighters operated by China’s People’s Liberation Army Air Force, with modern avionics, advanced radar and electronic warfare systems. According to Bloomberg, the J-16, built by AVIC Shenyang, is larger and heavier than the J-10, with twin engines and two seats, and is designed for longer-range missions. China sent J-10s to Eagles of Civilization in 2025.During its inaugural joint exercise with the North African country last year, China deployed J-10C fighters, which are lighter, single-engine multi-role jets.Song Zhongping, a Chinese military commentator and former PLA instructor, told SCMP that the journey to Egypt – the J-16’s longest-range deployment to date – would have been a “major test” for the pilots’ tactical and technical skills as well as the aircraft’s technical performance.According to the report, the planes and aviators taking part in the Eagles of Civilisation 2026 exercise arrived at an Egyptian airbase on Friday morning after a 6,000km (3,700-mile) journey that took 9 hours and required mid-air refuelling, according to the People’s Liberation Army.“A video attached to the PLA Air Force release, filmed through the window of a YY-20A aerial refueling aircraft, showed a Chinese J-16 fighter jet being refueled in mid-air. Another scene showed that the YY-20A hosted in-flight refueling for two J-16s at the same time. According to the release, the aerial refueling took place en route to Egypt,” Global Times reported.Egypt is a US strategic partner whose military operates American F-16 fighters as well as CH-47 Chinook and AH-64 Apache helicopters. It has maintained diplomatic relations with China for about seven decades, with ties deepening in recent years.
